summary:
Muse Spark is available through Meta's own "Meta Model API". Docs are at https://dev.meta.ai/docs, the base URL is https://api.meta.ai/v1, and auth is a Bearer key held in the MODEL_API_KEY env var. I confirmed the endpoint is live: GET /v1/status returns 200 "operational" and GET /v1/models without a key returns 401 invalid_api_key.

The API speaks three protocols:
- the native Responses API (/v1/responses)
- OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions (/v1/chat/completions)
- Anthropic-compatible Messages (/v1/messages)

Available features:
- Tool calling (tool_choice can only be "auto"; parallel calls are on by default; there is a strict flag)
- JSON-schema structured output: response_format in Chat Completions, text.format in Responses
- Image input as a URL, a base64 data: URL or a file_id. A ~1280px image costs ~1.3-1.5k tokens and a request takes up to 50 images.
- MP4 video input
- A 1,048,576-token context window

Current model ids:
- muse-spark-1.3, the recommended one, released 2026-09-02
- muse-spark-1.2 and muse-spark-1.1
- the cheap "-contributor" versions (muse-spark-1.3-contributor, muse-spark-1.2-contributor). On these, Meta may train on your prompts and completions.

Prices per million tokens:
- Standard: $1.25 in, $4.25 out, $0.15 cached
- Contributor: $0.10 in, $0.20 out, $0.002 cached

Rate limits are per team: Standard 3,000 RPM / 4M TPM, Contributor 100 RPM / 3M TPM.

Reasoning cannot be turned off. "none" returns a 400 and "minimal" is the lowest setting. Reasoning is hidden, so it arrives as delay before the first token. Artificial Analysis measures time to first token at about 34 s at xhigh effort. Nobody has published a latency figure for minimal effort, so a 1 call/s loop has to be measured before anything is promised.

The "$20 free credits for new accounts" claim comes only from press (CNBC via AI Weekly, layer3labs, studentoffers). None of Meta's pricing, billing or sign-up pages mention it, and sign-up asks you to add a payment method.

OpenRouter carries meta/muse-spark-1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 (plus contributor versions) at the same prices, and also meta/muse-glimmer-30b.

muse.ai is not an unrelated company today:
- WHOIS registrant is Meta Platforms, Inc. (record updated 2026-08-19).
- The site resolves to Meta IPs, its PWA manifest has id "meta_ai" and name "Muse", and it sits behind a Meta/Facebook login.
- Its robots.txt says: "Collection of data on Muse through automated means is prohibited unless you have express written permission from Muse".

Minimal request, verbatim from https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/chat-completions:
```
curl -X POST "https://api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions" -H "Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model": "muse-spark-1.3", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What are three differences between TCP and UDP?"}]}'
```
The Python version is OpenAI(base_url="https://api.meta.ai/v1", api_key=os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"]).chat.completions.create(model="muse-spark-1.3", messages=[...]). Add reasoning_effort="minimal" for low latency (per https://dev.meta.ai/docs/reasoning).

Research limits: the session's web-search budget ran out partway through. After that I could only fetch known URLs directly. I made no project file changes, and the temporary scratchpad downloads have been deleted.

Nav includes /docs/quickstart, /docs/authentication, /docs/models, /docs/pricing-rate-limits, /docs/tool-calling, /docs/structured-output, /docs/reasoning, /docs/image-understanding, /docs/video-understanding, /docs/protocols, /docs/api-reference, /docs/muse-code.

facts.claim: Three protocols run the same models at the same price: Responses POST /v1/responses (native, recommended for agents; keeps reasoning across tool turns via previous_response_id or encrypted replay), Chat Completions POST /v1/chat/completions (OpenAI-compatible), and Messages POST /v1/messages (Anthropic-compatible; for the Anthropic SDK the base is https://api.meta.ai). Works with the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, LangChain, LlamaIndex and the Vercel AI SDK.

Text model ids: muse-spark-1.3 (Standard, 'tuned for agentic workflows', recommended), muse-spark-1.3-contributor, muse-spark-1.2, muse-spark-1.2-contributor, muse-spark-1.1. All accept text, image, video, audio and PDF input, output text, and have a 1,048,576-token context window. Other models on the same API: muse-image-1.0, muse-voice-transcribe-1.0, sam-3.1.
Release dates: Muse Spark first released 2026-04-08; Muse Spark 1.1 API launched 2026-07-08/09 (Meta blog dated July 8, press July 9); 1.2 listed on OpenRouter 2026-08-05; 1.3 released 2026-09-02.

Price per 1M tokens. Standard (1.3/1.2/1.1): input $1.25, cached input $0.15, output $4.25. Contributor (1.3/1.2-contributor): input $0.10, cached $0.002, output $0.20. Web search grounding costs an extra $2.50 per 1,000 queries.

Contributor tier trade-off: 'heavily discounted token pricing in exchange for permission to use your prompts and completions to train future Meta models'. ToS 6.1 applies this to 'Discounted Services'.

Rate limits apply per team, not per key. Standard: 3,000 RPM and 4,000,000 TPM. Contributor: 100 RPM and 3,000,000 TPM. A breach returns HTTP 429. The docs give no spend-based tiers and no special limits for new accounts.
$20 in free credits for every new Model API account.

Meta's own pricing, billing and sign-up pages do not mention free credits. ToS 13.3 only says Meta 'may provide you with promotional credits'. Sign-up requires age 18+ and a supported country, then 'Add a payment method' and 'Create an API key'. So whether the $20 is still offered in October 2026, and whether it needs a card, is UNVERIFIED.

Tool calling works on Responses (flat tool definitions; 'function' and freeform 'custom' tools; built-in web_search and tool_search) and on Chat Completions (OpenAI 'function' nesting). Only tool_choice 'auto' is supported; any other value returns 400. Parallel tool calls are on by default (set parallel_tool_calls:false to turn off). Optional strict schemas.

Structured output: Chat Completions uses response_format {type:'json_schema', json_schema:{name, schema, strict}}; Responses uses text.format. It combines with tools and images. Limits: nesting depth 10, 5,000 properties, no recursive schemas. Strict mode needs additionalProperties:false and every key listed in required.

Parameters that return 400 on Chat Completions: stop, n>1, logprobs/top_logprobs, logit_bias, prediction, verbosity, web_search_options, modalities, audio. Supported: temperature, top_p, max_tokens/max_completion_tokens, seed, reasoning_effort, tools, response_format, parallel_tool_calls, prompt_cache_key, safety_identifier, stream.

Vision input works on Responses and Chat Completions, as a public URL, a base64 data: URL or a Files API file_id. Formats: jpeg, png, gif, webp, ico. Up to 50 images per request, 50 MB per inline image. A ~1280px image costs about 1,300-1,500 tokens; POST /v1/responses/input_tokens counts tokens exactly. There is no 'detail' parameter. MP4 video works via input_file.

Reasoning cannot be turned off. Muse Spark accepts minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max (Standard tier only); 'none' returns HTTP 400. If omitted, the model reasons at a model-determined level. Reasoning tokens are billed as output. The chain of thought is private (optional summary on Responses), so it shows up as delay before the first visible token.

Whether 'max' reasoning is usable differs by source. The research blog says max is available on Model API. The reasoning docs say max is Standard-tier only. DataCamp found it feature-gated in Muse Code, silently downgraded to xhigh.

Latency at xhigh effort, measured by Artificial Analysis: output ~219 tok/s and time to first token ~33.8 s. A search snippet of the same site showed 148 tok/s and 37 s, so the numbers move over time. No published figure exists for minimal or low effort.
DataCamp measured OpenRouter as slower than Meta's own endpoint: ~81 vs ~182 tok/s.
Meta claims 1.3 uses ~20% fewer tool calls and ~25% fewer tokens than 1.2. DataCamp's own 3-task test found a net cost increase of 12%.

OpenRouter lists meta/muse-spark-1.3, meta/muse-spark-1.3-contributor, meta/muse-spark-1.2, meta/muse-spark-1.2-contributor and meta/muse-spark-1.1. Prices match Meta's. Context 1,048,576, max completion 943,718, is_moderated true, sole provider Meta. Supported parameters: tools, tool_choice, response_format, structured_outputs, reasoning, reasoning_effort. Inputs: text, image, video, file.
OpenRouter also lists meta/muse-glimmer-30b. Context 131,072; $0.30 in / $1.20 out per 1M; text and image input; tools and structured outputs supported. Providers: Phala, DeepInfra (bf16), Together.

Muse Glimmer is a 30B dense multimodal model (text and image in, text out) under Apache 2.0, released 2026-08-10. Default context is 128K. Launch runtimes include llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and LM Studio. The docs page does not mention Apple MLX.

Availability: the API launched as a US-only preview in July 2026. The product page now says 'Public preview. Now available with expanded global access.' The Geographic Use Policy (updated 2026-09-18) lists Restricted Territories that include the People's Republic of China (with Hong Kong and Macau) and Russia, and bars Muse Image in India.

ToS (last updated 2026-10-02), section 10.1: 'You and your End Users must be at least 18 years of age to use the Services and Integrated Products, and you will not create Integrated Products targeted at individuals under the age of 18.' 10.1(v) bars making Integrated Products available in non-permitted countries.

ToS section 7: 'No trademark licenses are granted ... in connection with the Services, neither we nor you may use any name or mark owned by or associated with the other or any of its affiliates.' Section 10.1(xi) bars publishing benchmarks of the Services to promote a competing product without written permission.

The AUP forbids running AI agents 'in ways that evade human oversight or accountability'. It also forbids using the Services to 'autonomously interact with systems or services in a manner that violates the terms of service' of those systems, and failing to disclose material risks or limitations to End Users where law or harm-prevention requires it.

facts.claim: muse.ai is Meta's consumer Muse assistant (the former meta.ai web app). It may have artifacts, sharing and connectors: robots.txt lists /artifacts, /share, /connectors, /crons and /goals, and the CSP frames *.meta-agents-apps.workers.dev. What those features do is unknown because everything is behind login.
Muse Spark 1.1 has been available free in the Meta AI app and on meta.ai in Thinking mode (consumer use may be rate-limited).

Meta's launch blog shows Muse Spark running a computer-use agent ('screenshot, reason about the board, click, screenshot again', Minesweeper example). The cookbook recipe uses an MCP bridge with cua_screenshot, cua_left_click, cua_type_text, cua_press_key and cua_run_command, and works around the 50-images-per-request limit with sub-agents. The blog does not mention Minecraft.

rmalde/minecraft-agent (the Jev Ender Dragon run) reads text game state through Mineflayer, not pixels, on Minecraft Java 1.16.5. It calls models through OpenRouter's OpenAI-compatible /api/v1/chat/completions, selected by the PLANNER_MODEL env var; keys come from Google Secret Manager. The verified 8:43 run used 131 Jev decisions and 35 Astra calls, about 0.32 calls per second. No license is stated.
The local machine is an Apple M2 with 16 GB unified memory. Ollama is not installed; java is at /usr/bin/java.

implications: Fastest build: rmalde/minecraft-agent already calls an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint through OpenRouter. Pointing its planner (and possibly its action picker) at meta/muse-spark-1.3 on OpenRouter, or at https://api.meta.ai/v1 with model muse-spark-1.3, should be close to a config change. The user needs exactly one credential, a Meta Model API key or an OpenRouter key; it cannot be avoided for Spark, and creating it needs their card.

A 1-call-per-second loop is unproven. Hidden reasoning cannot be switched off (minimal is the floor) and Artificial Analysis measures ~34 s to first token at xhigh. Plan the agent as two layers: Muse Spark at minimal or low effort as the planner, a few times a minute; Mineflayer pathfinding or a scripted executor fills the gaps. The Jev run needed only ~0.32 calls/s in total. Measure minimal-effort latency before promising a speed on screen.

Cost at 1 call/s, my estimate (I did not measure token counts). Pixel loop at ~2.4k input + ~200 output tokens per call: Standard ≈ $0.004/call ≈ $14/hour, so $20 lasts ~1.5 hours; Contributor ≈ $0.0003/call ≈ $1/hour, so $20 lasts ~20 hours. Text-state loop (Mineflayer JSON, ~1.5k in / ~150 out): Standard ≈ $9/hour, Contributor ≈ $0.65/hour. A whole Ender-Dragon-style run (~170 calls) costs about $1-2 on Standard and about $0.10 on Contributor. Any large count of hidden reasoning tokens raises these numbers, because reasoning is billed as output.

Contributor tier is cheap enough for long runs but has two catches. Meta may train on everything sent, so viewer prompts must be disclosed and nothing private sent. Its 100 RPM team limit fits about one agent at 1 Hz, so a public try-it page with several viewers at once needs Standard tier (3,000 RPM) or a queue.

A public try-it page has legal limits. Meta's ToS requires End Users to be 18+ and forbids products aimed at under-18s, which matters for a Minecraft audience, so the page needs an 18+ gate. It also cannot be offered in the PRC, Hong Kong or Macau, so the Douyin cut can show the video but cannot link a playable demo for viewers in China. The page must never put the API key in the browser: use a server-side proxy, a per-viewer quota, a spend alert, a visible log and a stop button (the AUP's human-oversight rule).

Branding: ToS section 7 grants no trademark licence. Use plain descriptive wording ('powered by Meta's Muse Spark'), no Meta or Muse logos, and do not suggest Meta endorses the project. Run on our own local Minecraft server, not public servers, to stay inside the AUP rule about violating other services' terms. Whether 'Muse plays Minecraft' as a title is fine under ToS section 7 is a legal question (UNVERIFIED).

'Try it on muse.ai' cannot mean a bot driving the muse.ai web app: muse.ai is Meta's consumer Muse app and its robots.txt bans automated collection. The only path is a supported muse.ai feature (artifacts, connectors or MCP) that ordinary users turn on themselves; whether one exists is UNVERIFIED. Otherwise we host our own page that calls the API, and the video says 'Muse Spark via Meta's API'.

Pixels or text: Muse Spark takes screenshots (~1.4k tokens per 1280px frame, 50 images per request) and Meta ships a computer-use recipe. So a Muse that plays from pixels is possible and answers the main criticism of Jev (text game state, not pixels). It is also slower and costs more per call than Mineflayer text state.

Running Muse Glimmer locally on this M2 is probably not practical. It is a 30B dense model, and 4-bit weights are about 15-17 GB (my estimate) against 16 GB of unified memory. Use Glimmer through OpenRouter (Together, DeepInfra, Phala) instead, or treat it as the fast-picker comparison. Its 131K context and 16K max output on DeepInfra are enough for an action picker.

Lab angle for the X post: Muse Spark's hidden-reasoning latency and its 3,000 RPM / 4M TPM limits are exactly the serving story behind KVFlow (prefix caching for agents) and Yggdrasil. The reusable system prompt plus game state also suits Meta's cached-input price ($0.15 Standard, $0.002 Contributor). Use prompt_cache_key on Chat Completions or previous_response_id on Responses.

summary:
Muse Glimmer is real and open. Meta Superintelligence Labs released it on 2026-08-10 under Apache 2.0. It is a dense model of about 29.6B parameters (including a 1.8B vision encoder), takes text and images, outputs text, and has a 131K context. Weights are on Hugging Face at meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B (not gated), with an official GGUF repo and a DFlash drafter. Ollama, llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang and LM Studio all support it. The official 4-bit build is about 17 GB and is aimed at 24-32 GB GPUs.

This Mac cannot run it as it stands. It is a MacBook Air M2 with 16 GB RAM and only 4.2 GB of free disk. Every 4-bit build is 15.4 GB or more, and even the smallest 2-bit file (8.7-8.9 GB) is larger than the free disk. Freeing space would allow a 2-bit build (about 10 GB) at an estimated 5-7 tok/s. No M2 or 16 GB measurement has been published. At 2-bit, the quant's own notes say precise multi-step tool calls degrade first, and those are exactly what a Minecraft agent needs. On a base M3 Air with 24 GB, the 4-bit build measured only 4.33 tok/s.

A 24 GB GPU is the right host. One independent test on an RTX 4090 with Q4_K_M reported about 75 tok/s output and 3,100+ tok/s prompt reading, with a 130K context in 19.3 GB. Serve it with llama.cpp or Ollama and send requests from the Mac over the local network. vLLM does not fit well on a single 24 GB card.

Tool calling is solid on paper: MCP Atlas 75.5, and on the tau3-Banking tool-use test 24% versus Qwen3.6-27B's 17%. Weak spots: it trails Qwen on Terminal-Bench and GDPval, hallucinates more (82% rate), and independent tests show some tool-looping. There are a few runtime bugs: one Ollama issue (#18808) is still open, and one llama.cpp issue was fixed. No game or Minecraft results for any Muse model were found.

Most important finding: muse.ai IS Meta's. It is the consumer personal agent "Muse", launched 2026-09-08 and run on Muse Spark 1.3. Each user gets a cloud Linux computer with a Chromium browser that the user can watch and take over. So the user's "网页端的muse.ai" is the right product, not an unrelated company. Glimmer itself is not offered there. Browser Minecraft Classic (classic.minecraft.net) is live. Note: the session's web-search budget ran out partway through. The last checks were done by fetching pages directly, and some negatives (no Muse Minecraft demo yet, Glimmer's OpenRouter id) are marked UNVERIFIED.

facts.claim: Muse Glimmer was released 2026-08-10 by Meta Superintelligence Labs under Apache 2.0. It is a 30B dense open-weights model, distilled from Muse Spark's outputs (logit distillation), built for local agents. Meta says full precision needs over 55 GB and the ~4-bit build under 20 GB.

Architecture: about 29.6B total parameters, including a ~1.8B ViT-G/14 vision encoder (50 layers). The text decoder is dense with 52 layers, in a repeating pattern of 3 sliding-window layers (2048 tokens) then 1 full-attention layer (NoPE). 32 heads, 2 KV heads, head_dim 128, hidden size 6656, vocabulary 202,048. Input is text, image or video; output is text. Knowledge cutoff 2026-01-04.

Context length is 131,072 (config max_position_embeddings; model card says '131,072+'; Ollama says 128K; Artificial Analysis says 131k). The Hugging Face launch blog instead lists 'Context Window: 32,768 tokens, Max Tokens: 8,192', probably an example config.

Hugging Face ids: meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B (BF16, not gated, no login needed), meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF, meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-assistant (DFlash speculative-decoding drafter), and the meta-models/muse-glimmer collection. Community builds: bartowski/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF, unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF, mlx-community/Muse-Glimmer-30B-4bit, -OptiQ-4bit, -mxfp4 and -nvfp4, btbtyler09/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GPTQ-4bit, Preyazz/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4.

Official GGUF files: KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M 16.8 GB (recommended start), KQuant-Dynamic-Q4_K_XL 19.7 GB, mmproj vision 1.4 GB, DFlash drafter 1.6 GB. Memory for the 17 GB build: ~17 GB text-only, ~19 GB with vision, ~20 GB with vision and drafter. No BF16 GGUF. Needs llama.cpp build b10353 or newer; the chat template is embedded and --jinja is required. Stop tokens are 200001 and 200008.

bartowski GGUF sizes: IQ2_XXS 8.92 GB, IQ2_M 10.66, Q2_K 11.04, IQ3_M 13.11, Q3_K_M 13.96, IQ4_XS 15.44, Q4_K_M 17.31, Q5_K_M 20.11, Q6_K 23.41, Q8_0 29.61, BF16 55.73 GB. Q4_K_M is recommended for 24 GB.
Unsloth dynamic GGUFs: UD-IQ2_XXS 10.7 GB, UD-IQ2_M 12.3, UD-Q2_K_XL 12.4, UD-Q3_K_XL 13.4, UD-Q4_K_XL 15.9 GB. Unsloth recommends 2-bit for 16 GB systems and 3-4 bit for 24 GB.

MLX: mlx-community/Muse-Glimmer-30B-4bit (converted with mlx-vlm 0.6.12) has weights of roughly 16-18 GB and needs about 18-20 GB with a 32K KV cache. The OptiQ-4bit build is 18.6 GB plus a 3.8 GB BF16 vision sidecar.

facts.claim: Ollama: the official library has muse-glimmer:30b / :latest (18 GB, 128K, vision, tools, thinking) and muse-glimmer:30b-mlx (19 GB, MLX engine on Apple Silicon, where DFlash gives 1.5x-1.8x). There is also an 'ollama launch claude --model muse-glimmer' integration. Community 2-bit tags for 12-16 GB machines: iq2_m 9.8 GB, q2_k 11 GB, iq2_xs 8.7 GB. Their notes say that at 2-bit 'arithmetic and precise multi-step tool schemas degrade first'.
Ollama 0.32.7 added Muse Glimmer support.
facts.source: https://www.phoronix.com/news/Meta-Muse-Glimmer (seen only as a search excerpt, page not opened)

facts.claim: Ollama issue #18808 (opened 2026-10-05, still open): on Ollama 0.35.0, the Hugging Face GGUF references (hf.co/unsloth/...:UD-Q4_K_XL and hf.co/meta-models/...:Q4_K_XL) produce no response, likely a Jinja template problem. The official library tag was not tested in that issue.
llama.cpp issue #29613: Muse Glimmer ignored the json_schema response_format under --jinja (tool calls were not affected). It is closed with PR #29615, and the fix is noted in release b11246.

How tools work: tools are given as JSON schemas in the system prompt. The model writes calls in its own XML-style 'ATEM' format (<atem:function_calls><atem:invoke name=...><atem:parameter name=...>). Tool results come back in the 'tool' role wrapped in <tool_output name=...>. Reasoning goes to an 'assistant to=self' channel. Reasoning strength is low / medium / high / xhigh, default high. Runtimes translate this into OpenAI-style tool_calls; for vLLM use --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer.
Recommended sampling: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64.

Benchmarks reported by Meta: MCP Atlas 75.5, DeepSearch QA 74.6, tau3-Banking 23.5, WildClawBench 47.6, Gaia2 43.3, OSWorld-Verified 65.9, ScreenSpot Pro 75.4, TerminalBench 2.1 51.7, SWE-Bench Verified 76.0, SWE-Bench Pro 51.2, GPQA Diamond 83.5.

Artificial Analysis (independent): Intelligence Index 17. Tau3-Banking 24% versus Qwen3.6 27B's 17% ('among the best in its class' at tool use). But Terminal-Bench 2.1 is 52% versus 61%, GDPval-AA v2 953 Elo versus 1141, and the hallucination rate is 82% versus 49%. Hosted API: 117.8 output tok/s, $0.32 / $1.35 per M tokens, 4 providers.

Independent agent test (kingy.ai), MacBook Pro M4 Pro 24 GB, llama.cpp Metal, 16.76 GB GGUF: 14.40 tok/s text-only, but only 3.67 tok/s with the vision projector loaded. On 7 agent tasks: 3 pass, 2 partial, 2 fail, versus Qwen3.6-27B at 2 pass, 5 fail (Qwen produced malformed JSON tool arguments).

Independent agent test (rickyzzzzz), M1 Max 64 GB, Ollama MLX engine, nvfp4 build: Glimmer passed 12/12 core agent tasks but 24/30 on the extended suite, with 4 tool-looping failures. It was 2.1x slower overall than Qwen 3.8 27B, which passed 30/30.

Mac speeds. Meta's numbers (17 GB build): M4 Max 23.7 tok/s (37.8 with DFlash), M5 Max 26.6 (50.2), RTX 5090 74.9 (233.4). Independent, MacBook Air M3 24 GB, 17 GB build, llama.cpp: 4.33 tok/s output and 26.2 tok/s prompt reading (a 4,166-token prompt took 157 s before the first token). That source recommends 32 GB unified memory as the minimum.

Muse is Meta's consumer personal agent, launched 2026-09-08. The web app really is at muse.ai, as the user said ("网页端的muse.ai"). It is not meta.ai, which is a separate assistant product. Meta owns muse.ai now: its nameservers are Facebook's, its security headers reference meta.ai, and the login redirects to facebook.com. The old video-hosting company called muse.ai renamed itself Skiv (skiv.com) in March 2026.

Muse runs in a per-user cloud computer (Meta calls it "Secure VM"). A separate guard agent, Sentinel, approves every outgoing network request and every connector action. Muse is free up to a weekly usage limit; paid plans are Power ($20/month) and Maximum ($100/month). It needs an age of 18+ and is in the US, possibly also Canada (sources disagree). It runs on the web, iOS, Android, WhatsApp and a Mac app.

What matters for Minecraft:
- **Muse's own browser cannot play a canvas or WebGL game.** Meta says its browser sub-agent reads only an accessibility-tree snapshot (the page structure screen readers use). It cannot run JavaScript, and a canvas exposes nothing to that tree.
- **Muse can call our own HTTPS API.** Meta's help says Muse writes custom connectors for any service with an API or CLI. The VM runs scheduled jobs, and approvals can be set to "Allow for this site" or "Always allow", so repeated calls to our endpoint are supported by design. Nobody has tested it yet.
- **MCP is unclear for consumer Muse.** The official connector directory accepts MCP servers, and the coding tool Muse Code supports MCP. Whether a consumer can add an MCP server as a custom connector is contested between sources.
- **Muse for Mac does see pixels.** It takes screenshots and clicks through macOS Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions. That runs outside the web app, and it is untested on a real-time game like Minecraft Java.

How an ordinary viewer could play from muse.ai, ranked by feasibility:
1. **Our web page that Muse can read.** We host a page that shows the bot's world for humans and puts the game state in plain text with buttons for skills, all wired to a mineflayer bot on a real Minecraft server. The viewer pastes one prompt and approves the site once.
2. **A custom connector.** The viewer asks Muse to build a connector from our OpenAPI spec. It is more structured, but takes more setup and shows a warning that Meta does not review custom connectors.
3. Either of the above plus a scheduled task, for a long "Muse lives in Minecraft" run.
4. **An official directory connector** submitted at muse.ai/platform. This is the best experience for viewers, but review happens in waves with no stated timeline and requires business verification.
5. **Muse for Mac driving real Minecraft Java.** Good for one filmed stunt, not for the public.
6. Muse installing mineflayer inside its VM and connecting straight to our server. Sentinel's handling of non-HTTP traffic is unverified.
7. Not feasible: playing a canvas or WebGL Minecraft, including classic.minecraft.net, through Muse's browser.

The open-source Jev harness (rmalde/minecraft-agent) already uses this shape: mineflayer, a text game state, a small set of bounded skills, and model calls through an OpenAI-style interface. Meta's model API accepts the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs.

State of play on 2026-10-06. Web search ran out partway through, so everything after that point comes from fetching primary pages directly. Anything not confirmed at a source is marked UNVERIFIED.

(1) The "Jev plays Minecraft" post from Hao AI Lab (UCSD) is MCJev, a PvP bot. Viewers fight it by joining a public server (mc.alexzms.com) from their own Minecraft Java client. It has a mineflayer "body" running at 20 Hz and a Python "head". Each tick the head writes the fight as about 1,760 tokens of text and scores 16 to 20 moves in a single forward pass. The model behind it is not TypeSafe's hosted Jev. It is DJev, an open "Jev-style" decision server built on Google's DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B, and the lab got it to about 24 ms per decision on B200/GB200 GPUs (down from 174 ms). Over 32 hours, 54 players played 1,795 rounds. Jev won 70% of Block UHC rounds, and humans won 88% of Sumo rounds.

(2) TypeSafe's real Jev is a "System 1" model: you send a state plus typed questions and get back choices, probabilities and confidence. Separately, Ronak Malde's rmalde/minecraft-agent used GPT-6 Astra as planner, Jev as action picker and Mineflayer as executor. It beat the Ender Dragon in 8:43 for under $1, but on Java 1.16.5 with a fixed seed and a route surveyed in advance.

(3) Mindcraft (now mindcraft-bots/mindcraft, MIT, about 5.8k stars) is the quickest base for us. It supports Minecraft Java up to 1.21.11 (1.21.6 recommended). Its latest release is v0.1.4 (2026-03-20) and the last commit was 2026-10-03. It has about 19 provider modules, and a custom `url` turns the openai provider into a chat.completions client. Mineflayer 4.39.0 (2026-09-06) is tested on 1.8.8 through 26.1. The current Minecraft Java release is 26.3. Paper's stable build is 26.2. ViaVersion 5.12.0 lets 26.3 clients join older servers.

facts.claim: Hao AI Lab's X post reads: 'We let Jev play Minecraft. And we just can't beat it! Jev: 24 ms decisions. You: ~200 ms reactions. It moves before you even see it move ... (join the server to win)'. The video shows live PvP against real players.

facts.claim: The Hao AI Lab demo is MCJev (blog 'MCJev: Real-Time Decisions with Jev', published 2026-10-05; authors Minshen (Alex) Zhang ... Hao Zhang). The model is DJev, a 'Jev-style' structured-decision server by @mmastrac (from vLLM PR 57250), running on Google's DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B. It is not TypeSafe's hosted Jev API.

MCJev architecture: a mineflayer 'body' runs reflexes at 20 ticks/s (aim, arrow lead, dodge, lava/ledge guards). A Python 'head' writes the fight as about 1,760 tokens of text and scores 16 to 20 discrete moves in one decoder pass ('scoring, not generating'). It uses no pixels.

MCJev latency was about 24 ms per decision in real rounds on NVIDIA B200/GB200, versus 174 ms with HF transformers and about 60 ms with a leading engine (2.5x). That is roughly 6 ms fixed plus about 10.4 ms per 1k uncached tokens, using CUDA graphs, prefix-cache slots, FA2 and tuned Triton kernels. 8 GB200s served the public server at 362 decisions/s. The blog estimates a reasoning LLM at about 1 s per decision, which is too slow for 50 ms ticks.

MCJev public results: 54 people played 1,795 rounds in about 32 h. Jev won 70% of 870 Block UHC rounds, players won 88% of 925 Sumo rounds, and the fastest kill was 1.2 s. Prompt evolution went from v1 (lost all rounds) to v9 (won all scripted fights) in under 2 h without retraining.
The MCJev site lobby stats show a different win rate: about 83% of 348 rounds, versus 70% of Block UHC rounds in the blog. These are probably different snapshots.

Joining MCJev: Java Edition 1.9 or newer, a Microsoft account that owns the game, server address mc.alexzms.com, then right-click the lobby compass to pick a mode (Block UHC, Sumo, 2v2, Sudden Death). Self-hosting needs a Minecraft Java 1.11.2 Paper/Spigot server with online-mode=false and an NVIDIA GPU with about 50 GB. Apache-2.0. Mac is not supported.

TypeSafe's Jev is a 'System One' model. Input is state plus typed questions (Choice, Score, Noul, evaluated in parallel). Output is typed answers with probabilities and confidence instead of autoregressive text. Jev launched around 2026-09-15.
TypeSafe raised a $40M seed led by DCVC on 2026-09-15. The founder is an ex-OpenAI researcher whose name is given as 'Diego Almeida' in one source and 'Diogo Almeida' in another.
An early developer Jev Minecraft bot reportedly ran for 2 minutes on about 150k tokens for about 1 cent.
'Jev Plays Minecraft' is a 24/7 Twitch livestream (twitch.tv/jevplaysminecraft) in which Jev attempts the Ender Dragon one decision at a time. It was listed 2026-09-17.

rmalde/minecraft-agent: GPT-6 Astra (or GPT-5.6 Sol) plans via OpenRouter, JEV-1.13 picks bounded actions, and Mineflayer does pathfinding and protocol. Java 1.16.5. Latest run 'nether-final-08' killed the dragon in 8:43.3 with 131 Jev and 35 Astra calls, at about $0.01 Jev + $0.96 Astra. Fixed seed 8398967436125155523 with a route surveyed in a separate test world. 579 stars. No license file, so reusing its code needs permission.

The sources disagree on how rmalde's agent controls the player. Ronak Malde's X post says Jev controls WASD, space, click and mouse. The repo README says 'structured-state control, not control from screenshots or individual key presses' through Mineflayer.
Before Astra+Jev, an Astra-only livestream (Vals AI) ran 141 h without finishing the game and fell into potato farming.
teknium1/hermes-and-jev-play-minecraft is another stack (Hermes Agent plans, Jev picks, Mineflayer executes). It reproduces rmalde's dragon run. MIT, created 2026-09-21.
Mindcraft's canonical repo is now mindcraft-bots/mindcraft (kolbytn/mindcraft redirects there). MIT, 5,846 stars. Latest release v0.1.4 (2026-03-20). Last commit 2026-10-03.

Mindcraft supports Minecraft Java up to v1.21.11 and recommends v1.21.6. It recommends Node v18/v20 LTS and warns that 'Node v24+ may cause issues with native dependencies'. It depends on mineflayer ^4.33.0, mineflayer-pvp, pathfinder, collectblock and prismarine-viewer.

Mindcraft provider modules in src/models: azure, cerebras, claude, deepseek, gemini, gpt (openai), grok, groq, huggingface, hyperbolic, lmstudio, mercury, mistral, novita, ollama, openrouter, qwen, replicate, vllm.

To add an OpenAI-compatible model in Mindcraft, set the profile's model to an object {api:'openai', model, url, params}. With a url set, gpt.js uses chat.completions with OPENAI_API_KEY and sends `stop` unless the model name contains 'o1', 'o3' or '5'. The name 'muse-spark-1.3' contains none of these, so `stop` would be sent.

Mindcraft settings: default host 127.0.0.1, port 55916 (open a world to LAN on that port), auth 'offline', mindserver UI port 8080. allow_insecure_coding, allow_vision, speak and render_bot_view are all false by default. If the embedding model fails, it falls back to word-overlap.

Mindcraft security and accounts: 'Do not connect this bot to public servers with coding enabled ... vulnerable to injection attacks.' For online servers the bot needs its own official Microsoft/Minecraft account, plus a second account if you want to play alongside it.

Mineflayer's latest release is 4.39.0 (2026-09-06). Tested versions run from 1.8.8 to 1.21.11 plus 26.1, with 26.1 as latestSupportedVersion. Java Edition only. Auth options are offline and microsoft. prismarine-viewer gives a live browser view of the bot (first-person or bird's-eye).

It is effectively unmaintained.
MineDojo (MIT, 2.3k stars, last push 2024-03) is a 2022 benchmark framework that is effectively unmaintained. Its Minecraft version (believed to be 1.11.2 via Malmo) was not checked.
The current Minecraft Java release is 26.3 'Wilderness Bound' (2026-09-15), with 26.4 in snapshot. Mojang moved to year-based version numbers in 2026 (26.1 in March, 26.2 'Chaos Cubed' in June).

None of this could be checked because minecraft.net timed out three times.

muse.ai IS Meta's Muse personal AI agent web app. It is also on iOS, Android and WhatsApp, launched in the US on 2026-09-08 and is powered by Muse Spark. Built-in connectors include email, WhatsApp, Instagram and Link by Stripe.

Muse needs a Meta account with phone verification but no Facebook or Instagram. It has a free tier plus Power ($20/mo) and Maximum ($100/mo). Meta has also said Muse 'stays free' with a large token allowance.

Sources disagree on whether consumer Muse accepts a remote MCP URL (streamable HTTP + OAuth) or only services with their own REST API or CLI.

Muse Connector Platform (directory listing): a 3-step form at muse.ai/platform asking for an MCP or raw-API endpoint, auth, a privacy policy and ToS. Meta reviews each connector for functional, security and legal requirements. There were 1,500 to 2,000+ applications in the first week, onboarded 'in waves over the coming weeks'.
Muse for Mac was released 2026-09-18. Full computer control ('drive any app on your Mac') was announced at Meta Connect on 2026-09-23. Its speed and whether it works with games were not documented.

Meta Model API: OpenAI-compatible at https://api.meta.ai/v1 (chat.completions and responses), plus Anthropic-compatible messages. Model ids are muse-spark-1.1, 1.2 and 1.3; 1.1 is the default, so pass 1.3 explicitly. Public preview for US developers; sign up at dev.meta.ai.

Muse Spark API pricing is $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens, with $20 in free credits. Muse Spark 1.1 shipped 2026-07-09. The free-credit figure comes from secondary sources only.

The Meta chat-completions endpoint rejects `stop`, `n>1`, `logprobs`/`top_logprobs`, `web_search_options` and audio with HTTP 400. It supports tools/tool_choice, response_format (JSON schema), reasoning_effort ('none' not supported on Muse Spark), prompt_cache_key, seed and streaming.

Muse Glimmer (released 2026-08-10) is a 30B dense multimodal (text and image) model distilled from Muse Spark. Apache 2.0, 128K context. It runs on Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM and SGLang, and is hosted on Together, Fireworks and OpenRouter. Meta lists 24 to 32 GB GPUs or M4-Max/M5-Max Macs.

The smallest Muse Glimmer GGUF is Q4_K_M at 16.8 GB (about 17 GB with context, about 19 GB with vision). A MacBook Air M3 with 24 GB measured 4.33 tok/s generation and 157 s time-to-first-token on a 4k prompt. 32 GB is recommended.
This session's Mac is an Apple M2 with 16 GB RAM on macOS 15.5. No Java runtime is installed, Node is v25.2.1, and Ollama is not installed.

implications: Don't compete with Jev on reflex speed. Muse Spark is a reasoning model with no `none` effort and no logprobs, so it cannot copy Jev's score-every-option-in-one-pass trick. Hao AI Lab itself puts reasoning LLMs at about 1 s per decision. Position Muse as the System-2 brain (talks, plans, builds from a description) on top of mineflayer reflexes (pathfinder, pvp, collectblock). That is the Mindcraft pattern.

Fastest working build: Mindcraft with Muse Spark 1.3 as the model {api:'openai', model:'muse-spark-1.3', url:'https://api.meta.ai/v1'}, the Meta key in OPENAI_API_KEY, and params {reasoning_effort:'low'} to cut latency. Patch gpt.js so it does not send `stop`, because the Meta API returns 400 on it and Mindcraft only drops it for names containing o1/o3/5. This is a one-line fix, or use a tiny local proxy that strips the field.

Environment work on this Mac before anything runs: install Node 20/22 (nvm) because the current v25 conflicts with Mindcraft's native deps (canvas, gl), and install a Java runtime for the server. A Paper server on 1.21.6 (Mindcraft's recommended version, inside Mineflayer's range) plus ViaVersion 5.12 lets viewers on the newest 26.3 client join.

Muse Glimmer cannot run locally on this 16 GB M2: the smallest file is 16.8 GB and 24 GB Macs manage about 4 tok/s. For an 'open weights' episode, call hosted Glimmer through Mindcraft's built-in openrouter provider (model id UNVERIFIED) and say so on screen. Otherwise it needs a 32 GB+ Mac or a 24 GB GPU.

'Try it from muse.ai' is plausible but not proven. Expose a small public HTTPS API from the Mac (tunnel, bearer token, OpenAPI spec, whitelisted actions such as build/follow/collect, rate limits). A viewer then tells their Muse to create a custom connector to it, and the bot acts in our world while they watch a stream or a prismarine-viewer page. A REST + OpenAPI design works under both conflicting accounts of what Muse accepts. Test it in a real muse.ai account first. It is US-only, so the Douyin cut needs a different call to action.

The proven way to let viewers play is Hao AI Lab's 'join the server' approach. The server should run with online-mode=true, and the bot then needs its own Microsoft account that owns Java Edition (cost unverified). Offline-mode is acceptable only for local filming. Keep allow_insecure_coding=false, because chat from strangers is a prompt-injection path. Hosting the server from the Mac at UCSD/home needs a tunnel or port forwarding. Network policy is unverified.

What goes viral in this genre: one hard number on frame 0 (8:43 dragon; <$1; 24 ms vs ~200 ms human), an open invitation to play (MCJev: 54 players, 1,795 rounds in 32 h), a 24/7 livestream, and honest failure comedy (Astra's 141 h of potato farming). A Muse version should open with its own number: for example, one sentence typed into muse.ai produces a finished build in N minutes for $X of Muse tokens.

Honest framing: Hao AI Lab's 'Jev' is really DJev on DiffusionGemma, and rmalde's run used a fixed seed and a surveyed route. Hold our claims to the same standard: measured times and costs, show the seed/setup, and do not claim 'first' until it is checked.

Lab angle with real measurements: Mindcraft resends a long system prompt every turn, and the Meta API exposes prompt_cache_key. A KVFlow-style prefix-caching story could measure latency and cost per decision with caching on and off. MCJev's 6 ms + 10.4 ms per 1k uncached tokens is a ready reference curve.

Filming: prismarine-viewer (already a Mindcraft dependency; render_bot_view) gives a browser bird's-eye or first-person view of the bot for overlays. The hero shots should come from a real client capture by the user, because the house rule prefers real assets. Code licenses are safe to build on: Mindcraft MIT, Mineflayer MIT, MCJev Apache-2.0, ViaVersion GPL-3.0 as a plugin, Glimmer Apache-2.0. rmalde/minecraft-agent has no license, so do not reuse its code.

summary: I found no public project where a Meta Muse model plays Minecraft or any other game. That covers Muse Spark through the API and Muse Glimmer with open weights. I searched GitHub repos and code, Hacker News and the web, and checked the MineTrials Minecraft benchmark, which doesn't include Muse. "Muse plays Minecraft" therefore looks like a first, but this is unconfirmed: X search needs a login, and the session's shared web-search budget (200 calls) ran out before I could search Reddit, YouTube or the X replies. Three findings change the plan. (1) The user was right about muse.ai. It is Meta's own domain: WHOIS lists Meta Platforms as the registrant, and the site runs on Meta's servers. It hosts "Muse", Meta's personal AI agent, which launched in the US on Sept 8, 2026 and runs on Muse Spark. Each user's Muse has its own cloud VM with a browser, it can run code, and it can add MCP "custom connectors" (MCP is the standard way to plug tools into an agent). So a viewer could genuinely play from muse.ai: they add our Minecraft connector, give an order, and watch the result in a browser. The catch is that the Muse app reportedly needs a US account, age 18+ and a payment card on file. (2) The Mac here is an Apple M2 with 16 GB of memory. The smallest official Muse Glimmer file is 16.76 GB, and LM Studio says it needs at least 26 GB of RAM, so Glimmer cannot run on this machine. The model will have to be Muse Spark through the API, or Glimmer on a bigger machine. (3) The Hao AI Lab "Jev plays Minecraft" post did modestly: 112K views, 1,059 likes, 42 replies. The original viral Jev Minecraft post was Ronak Malde's "Jev + Astra beats the Ender Dragon in 8:43 for under $1" (Sept 20), with 2.1M views. Hao's bot is not TypeSafe's Jev at all. It is Google's DiffusionGemma-26B used as a Jev-style decision model on NVIDIA B200 GPUs. Its playable server needed a paid Minecraft Java account, and only 54 people played. The best-spreading "AI plays a game" demos share four things: one number set against a human or a clock (8:43 and under $1; 24 ms vs your 200 ms; Pokemon finished after 813 h), a story with a character, a way for viewers to join, and open code. The criticism they draw is always the same: "the harness does the work" or "it reads text, not pixels".

One decision took 174 ms in Hugging Face transformers, about 60 ms on a leading inference engine, and about 24 ms on their own engine (DJev-serve). MCJev public results: 54 people played 1,795 rounds in 32 hours (Sept 26-28). The bot won 70% of Block UHC rounds, but humans won 88% of 925 Sumo rounds. Joining required Minecraft Java Edition with a paid Microsoft account. The blog went up Oct 5, and the repo has 3 stars.

Cost less than $1 ($0.01 Jev, $0.96 Astra)', posted Sept 20, 2026, with open code. It has 2,098,366 views, 7,940 likes, 515 reposts, 259 replies, 280 quotes and 4,438 bookmarks, from an account with only 11,236 followers. Before the Ender Dragon run, Astra alone spent 141 hours (mostly farming potatoes) and went viral with a 'cute' story of an AI seemingly frustrated after losing its bed.

TypeSafe's 'Introducing System One Models and Jev' launch reached 1,989 points and 520 comments on Hacker News (Sept 15, 2026). Jev returns typed choices with scores rather than writing text, takes 70-500 ms end to end, and reads game state as text, not images.

A wave of Jev projects followed: madewithjev.com lists 755, 74 of them games. Open copies hit the Hacker News front page: Ollaya (618 points), Jeff 0.8B (575), Kev (463). 'Show HN: Jev Plays Pokémon Red' got 282 points and 124 comments (Sept 25). Critics there said the harness does the work ('builds a collision grid, computes reachable paths with A-star ... choices already annotated') and pointed to bad move choices.

Claude Plays Pokémon streamed on Twitch from the Claude 3.7 Sonnet launch (Feb 24-25, 2025). Anthropic's launch post said 3.7 Sonnet 'outperformed all previous models in our Pokémon gameplay tests'. Viewer numbers were not retrieved.

Gemini Plays Pokémon was run by an independent developer, Joel Zhang (@TheCodeOfJoel), from Mar 25, 2025. It finished Pokémon Blue on May 2, 2025 after about 813 hours; a second run took about 406 hours. Its harness combined screenshots with game-memory text, a minimap and helper agents. GPT-5 / o3 Pokémon runs in 2025: details (step counts, dates, reach) not checked this pass.

Mindcraft (Minecraft bots built on LLMs plus mineflayer) has 5,846 stars and supports Minecraft Java up to 1.21.11. A model can be set as {api:'openai', model, url}, so in principle it can point at api.meta.ai/v1. This has not been tested with Muse.

Similar 'Claude plays Minecraft' projects drew little attention: one Claude Agent SDK bot with MCP tools (5 HN points, Jan 2026) and ClaudeCraft, a public server where Claude bots do everything while people watch and give orders (4 points, Feb 2026). MineTrials also got 2 points.

implications: Build plan: muse.ai can be the front door. Lab hardware (the M2 is enough for a Paper server, a mineflayer bot and the web viewer) runs a Minecraft world, a bot and an MCP server that exposes the actions (go to, mine, craft, build, look). A viewer in muse.ai says 'Build a custom integration to Picasso MC, MCP URL ...', then 'go find diamonds', and watches the bot in a prismarine-viewer page. The video shows a real person's Muse doing it.

Muse's own VM is a second route if Sentinel lets it reach a Minecraft server port: Muse could install mineflayer and join our server with no connector at all. That would make 'Muse plays Minecraft' the most literal, but it needs a test.

Hao's participation hook failed on friction: 112K views produced only 54 players, because joining needed a paid Minecraft Java account. Our version should need zero installs: watch in a browser and command from muse.ai or a lab web page.

The Muse app is reportedly US-only, 18+ and needs a card on file, so most X viewers and every Douyin viewer can't use muse.ai. Ship a lab-hosted fallback page (watch plus a rate-limited command box that calls Muse Spark on the lab's API key) and present muse.ai as the US path.

Glimmer does not fit the M2 (16.76 GB file vs 16 GB RAM, 26 GB+ recommended). Use Muse Spark through the API (cheap; the $0.10/$0.20 contributor tier trains Meta on our prompts, so say so if we use it), or run Glimmer on a 24-32 GB GPU or Mac. A 'Glimmer runs locally' angle needs other hardware.

summary:
Ranked for a Muse-plays-Minecraft demo where the lab's own project is what runs on screen. Two facts set the ranking. First, this Mac is a base Apple M2 with 16 GB RAM (checked locally with sysctl). Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B model, and its official 4-bit build is about 17 GB, so it does not fit. Only 2-3 bit builds of 12-15 GB would load, and M2 memory bandwidth (100 GB/s) caps decoding at about 8 tok/s at best, so real-time local Glimmer on this machine is not realistic. Second, muse.ai and the Muse Spark API both run on Meta's servers, so none of our serving systems (KVFlow, ScaleSim, FastTree, Yggdrasil, SmoothAgent) can speed them up. Those systems only show a win where we serve Glimmer ourselves, in practice on an NVIDIA GPU, because every one of their codebases is built on CUDA, SGLang or Triton.

Ranking:
(1) FlashEvolve, NeurIPS'26. Speeds up agent self-evolution (GEPA-style prompt evolution). Public code, and it only needs an OpenAI-compatible client, so it can call api.meta.ai/v1 (Spark) from this Mac with no GPU. It lines up with Hao AI Lab's MCJev: their bot's prompt went through 8 hand-supervised versions in the first hour and reached v10 in about 9 hours. It is also the only project whose result reaches muse.ai viewers, as the evolved strategy or skill.
(2) KVFlow + ScaleSim, NeurIPS'25 / ICML'26, one public repo (Apache-2.0, SGLang 0.5.2rc1 fork). Workflow-aware KV cache eviction and prefetch for a planner+picker pair, or for a village of many Muse bots. This is the strongest systems story, but it needs Glimmer on our own NVIDIA GPU and a rebase onto a newer SGLang.
(3) SmoothAgent / Lookahead Context Engineering. Removes the long pauses (up to 11.9x time-to-first-token) when a long-running agent compacts its context. Very visual: the bot freezes vs. keeps moving. No public code found.
(4) FastTree, MLSys'25. Tree-shared-prefix attention kernel. Public artifact, but Triton tuned for H100.
(5) Yggdrasil, NeurIPS'25. Tree speculative decoding. No public code found; Glimmer already ships Meta's own DFlash drafter; and Jev-style one-pass decisions generate no tokens to speculate on.
(6) Pancake / HedraRAG. Agent memory and RAG. Weak on screen; no code found.
(7) Patterns behind Chaos, ISCA'26 Best Paper. Not usable: Glimmer is dense and Spark is closed.
Quantum work: not relevant.

Notes: muse.ai is confirmed as Meta's consumer Muse agent, not the old video company. It redirects to auth.muse.ai and then facebook.com, and Meta's newsroom names muse.ai. The lab publications page could not be read directly (it is a Google Sites embed), so the list came from the repo's pub/pub.html (served at yil384.github.io/Picasso-Lab/pub/pub.html) and social/x/pubs.json (136 entries). The web-search budget ran out partway through, so a few items below are marked UNVERIFIED.

facts.claim: This machine is a base Apple M2 with 17179869184 bytes (16 GB) of RAM on macOS 15.5. No ollama, llama-server or LM Studio is installed and MLX is not importable; Java and Node are present.
facts.source: local: sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string hw.memsize; sw_vers; which

facts.claim: M2 has 100 GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.

Muse Glimmer: released 2026-08-10, about 30B (29.6B) parameters, DENSE (not MoE), 52 layers, [Local,Local,Local,Global] attention with a 2048-token sliding window, gated attention, 131k context, vision encoder, Apache 2.0, Hugging Face meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B, no gating.
Glimmer has 32 query heads and 2 KV heads, about 52 KiB of KV cache per token in BF16, so its KV cache is very small.

Glimmer's official 4-bit build is 'under 20 GB' and is sized for a 24-32 GB envelope; Meta demoed it on M4 Max / M5 Max. Unsloth GGUFs: UD-Q2_K_XL 12-14 GB, UD-Q3_K_XL 14-15 GB, UD-Q4_K_XL 17 GB; a third party reports IQ2_M at 12.3 GB.
Glimmer ships a DFlash-based block drafter for speculative decoding: 3.1x on RTX 5090, 1.8x on M5 Max, 1.5x on M4 Max (Meta's numbers).
Glimmer runtimes: llama.cpp, MLX, ExecuTorch, plus partners Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth, vLLM, SGLang, Together, Fireworks, OpenRouter.

Glimmer speed on a 16 GB base M2 is untested. Bandwidth alone caps decoding at about 100/12.3 ≈ 8 tok/s for a 12.3 GB quant (my estimate). Prefill of a dense 30B on a base M2 is likely tens of tok/s, i.e. seconds to tens of seconds per 1-2k-token observation without a prefix cache.
facts.source: estimate from https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2022/06/apple-unveils-m2-with-breakthrough-performance-and-capabilities/ and the quant sizes above

facts.claim: Muse Spark API (Meta Model API, public preview): base URL api.meta.ai/v1, compatible with the OpenAI SDK and Anthropic Messages, model id muse-spark-1.1, $1.25 / $4.25 per M input/output tokens, reasoning_effort minimal..xhigh, image/video input.
New Meta Model API sign-ups get $20 of one-time free credits; the preview is for US developers only.
The Spark API caches prompt prefixes automatically (cached input about $1.00/M vs $1.25/M) and supports top_logprobs 'where supported'.
Third parties mention Muse Spark versions 1.2 and 1.3; Meta's own developer blog says muse-spark-1.1.

muse.ai is the web app of Meta's consumer Muse agent (launched 2026-09-08, powered by Muse Spark, runs a 'Muse Secure VM' that can open a browser). Fetching https://muse.ai redirects to auth.muse.ai and then to facebook.com, so the domain is Meta's.
facts.source: https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-personal-ai-agent/ ; WebFetch of https://muse.ai (307 to auth.muse.ai, 302 to facebook.com)

facts.claim: Muse consumer availability: US-only, 18+ (Meta / TechNode) vs. 'US and Canada', including a Mac desktop app (Zapier).
Muse consumer pricing: free tier plus $20 and $100 plans (TechNode, parallel.ai) vs. $16 Power / $80 Maximum (Zapier).
Consumer Muse can build Custom Connectors to a remote MCP server or OpenAPI/CLI, including on the free tier. A server on the user's own laptop is NOT reachable because the VM runs in Meta's cloud.

Hao AI Lab's MCJev (Apache-2.0): DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B scores about 20 moves in one forward pass with no generated tokens, about 24 ms per decision on B200/GB200. It reuses a prefix cache inside the CUDA graph. Its mineflayer body plus Python head call POST /api/evaluate. It needs an NVIDIA GPU with about 50 GB.

MCJev's prompt evolution was hand-supervised: an LLM reads the game logs and drafts a new prompt, and humans review it. That gave 8 harness versions in the first hour and v10 in about 9 hours. Jev won 70% of 870 Block UHC rounds; 54 people played 1,795 rounds.
The Hao AI Lab X post went up about 2026-09-27 (runtimewire); the blog post is dated 2026-10-05.

rmalde/minecraft-agent: a GPT-6 Astra planner plus a Jev picker choosing from 5-10 actions, mineflayer body, structured state (not pixels), Minecraft 1.16.5, models via OpenRouter, Ender Dragon in about 8:43. The README states no license.

The lab publications page (yufeiding.ucsd.edu/publications) could not be read by fetch because it is a Google Sites embed. Its source is pub/pub.html in this repo, served at yil384.github.io/Picasso-Lab/pub/pub.html, plus social/x/pubs.json (136 entries).

FlashEvolve (NeurIPS'26): an asynchronous worker-queue framework (Rollout/Reflect/Propose/Evaluate stages) for agent evolution (GEPA, ACE, Meta-Harness, OpenEvolve...). 3.5x proposal throughput vs GEPA on vLLM and 4.9x via API; IFBench 91% in 39.3 vs 104 min.
FlashEvolve code is public at github.com/Leo9660/FlashEvolve: 'OpenAI-compatible client only' at its core, vLLM optional. GitHub API shows 7 stars, last push 2026-07-30, and no license detected.

KVFlow (NeurIPS'25): an Agent Step Graph with steps-to-execution eviction plus overlapped CPU-to-GPU KV prefetch. Up to 1.83x on single workflows and 2.19x on concurrent workflows vs SGLang with hierarchical radix cache.

KVFlow and ScaleSim share one public repo, github.com/PanZaifeng/KVFlow (Apache-2.0, 32 stars, last push 2026-03-12). It is a fork of SGLang 0.5.2rc1 plus an 'SScheduler' layer the application calls to expose agent metadata. It handles priority eviction and prefetch for KV and per-agent LoRA. ScaleSim code was released 2026-02.
ScaleSim (ICML'26): 'invocation distance' estimates the order in which agents will call next, for prefetch and eviction in large LLM multi-agent simulations. Up to 1.74x vs SGLang.
SGLang now lists Apple Silicon support via Metal/MLX (SGLANG_USE_MLX=1). Its docs say nothing about radix/HiCache, LoRA or speculative decoding on that path.
SGLang 0.5.2rc1 (KVFlow's base) predates Glimmer (released 2026-08-10), so running Glimmer on KVFlow likely needs a rebase or a ported model file (my inference from the dates).
llama-server has per-slot prompt-cache endpoints (/slots/{id}?action=save|restore|erase with --slot-save-path; cache_prompt). Open issue #26676 reports that restore after a server restart is a no-op.

SmoothAgent / Lookahead Context Engineering (Pan, Wang, Hu, Chen, Guan, Zhou, Swanson, Ding): runs context transformations (offload, reduce, isolate) ahead of time and prepares transformed KV caches, cutting time-to-first-token by up to 11.9x. No code link on arXiv.

FastTree (MLSys'25): tree-structured shared-prefix attention kernels as an SGLang plugin (Triton, tuned for H100), up to 2.2x throughput. Artifact at github.com/PanZaifeng/FastTree-Artifact (Apache-2.0, last push 2025-03-24).
Yggdrasil (NeurIPS'25): latency-optimal tree speculative decoding on PyTorch/TorchInductor, up to 3.98x over Eagle/MeSpec. No public code repository found.

Patterns behind Chaos (ISCA'26 Best Paper): forecasts MoE expert data movement for large-scale (200B-1000B) MoE serving, including wafer-scale. Traces are at huggingface.co/datasets/core12345/MoE_expert_selection_trace. Nothing addresses consumer GPUs or Macs.
Pancake (arXiv'26): hierarchical ANN-index memory for multi-agent agent memory, more than 4.29x throughput. No code link.
Muse Spark's architecture (dense or MoE) is undisclosed.

implications: RANK 1 - FlashEvolve. Have Muse teach itself a Minecraft task with our evolution engine. The FlashEvolve client points at api.meta.ai/v1 (muse-spark-1.1) and runs entirely from this M2 Mac: no GPU, no server changes. Rollout = one mineflayer episode (e.g. Sumo vs a scripted bot, survive a night, collect N logs in T minutes); Reflect/Propose = Muse rewriting its own harness prompt from its logs. That is exactly MCJev's hand-supervised loop, automated and run asynchronously. On screen: score vs wall-clock, FlashEvolve vs synchronous GEPA; a v1 to vN prompt stack; 4-8 bots playing parallel rollouts. One measured number: minutes to reach the target score. It is the only lab project whose output reaches muse.ai viewers: the evolved prompt/skill is what a viewer's Muse uses. Wiring difficulty: MEDIUM (about 2-4 days): a scored Minecraft task and evaluator, a rollout stage wrapping a mineflayer episode, a local Paper server (Java and Node are present). Cost check: at $1.25/M input, 5,000 decisions x 1.5k tokens ≈ $9 of input before output and reasoning tokens. That fits the $20 credit only with reasoning_effort=minimal and short observations (my estimate).

RANK 2 - KVFlow + ScaleSim (one public repo). The headline systems story: Glimmer serving a multi-agent Minecraft setup, either a planner+picker pair (rmalde-style) or a 'Muse village' of 20-50 Glimmer bots with their own personas (ScaleSim's case). On screen: decisions/s or seconds per round for the village with KVFlow vs stock SGLang LRU, plus a per-bot cache-hit overlay. Caveats: (a) it cannot touch Spark or muse.ai, which run on Meta's servers; (b) the code is CUDA SGLang 0.5.2rc1 and likely needs a rebase for Glimmer; (c) Glimmer's KV is tiny (about 52 KiB/token), so eviction only matters with many agents x long contexts. You need a GPU of about 24-48 GB and 20+ bots for the gap to show. Difficulty: MEDIUM-HIGH on an NVIDIA GPU (about 1 week incl. rebase); HIGH on this Mac. On the Mac the only route is a 'KVFlow-lite' proxy that applies the Agent Step Graph policy through llama-server slot save/restore, and Glimmer barely fits in 16 GB.

RANK 3 - SmoothAgent / Lookahead Context Engineering. For a long-running Muse survival run (hours), every context compaction makes the bot freeze while the model re-reads the context; this paper hides it (up to 11.9x lower time-to-first-token). Very visual: split screen, the bot stops vs keeps moving. Code not public: ask Zaifeng Pan. The full version needs our own server (Glimmer on GPU). With Spark, a client-side lookahead (summarize earlier segments in the background and swap in when ready) can hide the summarization call but not Meta's re-prefill. Difficulty: HIGH without the authors' code.

RANK 4 - FastTree. Applies when many requests share a tree of prefixes: N bots sharing a world-state prefix, or scoring K multi-token action options as branches. Public artifact, but Triton tuned for H100, an older SGLang, and Glimmer's sliding-window/gated attention would need kernel work. No path on a Mac (no Triton/CUDA on Metal). Difficulty: HIGH; visible gain only on an NVIDIA GPU at scale.

RANK 5 - Yggdrasil. Speculative decoding helps only the planner's longer text, not Jev-style picking (one forward pass, zero generated tokens). Glimmer already ships Meta's DFlash drafter (1.5-3.1x), which we would have to beat on camera. No public code found. Difficulty: HIGH; weak story.

RANK 6 - Pancake (multi-agent memory search) and HedraRAG (retrieval for a skill library). Plausible for a village with long-term memory, but the speedup is invisible at Minecraft scale and no code was found. Skip for this demo.

NOT USABLE - Patterns behind Chaos (MoE best paper): Glimmer is dense, Spark is closed and its architecture is undisclosed. Keep it for the Strata/MoE posts. Quantum papers, chip/kernel work (ChipMATE, TritonGym, TLX, Proton, AMMA, Syncopate) and JigsawRL (RL post-training needs big GPUs; no code verified) do not fit this demo.

HARDWARE: this Mac is a base M2 with 16 GB. Glimmer's official 4-bit build (about 17 GB) does not fit, and 2-3 bit builds (12-15 GB) leave almost no room for the OS, the Minecraft client and the KV cache. Realistic split: Spark API = the Muse that plays (plus FlashEvolve) on this Mac; Glimmer + KVFlow/ScaleSim = a second film beat that needs an NVIDIA GPU (lab or cloud) or a Mac with 32 GB or more. Do not promise 'Muse runs locally on a Mac M2' on camera.

LATENCY: Spark is a reasoning model behind a network API, so per-decision latency is likely seconds (UNVERIFIED). Pick tasks that tolerate slow decisions (building, survival planning, turn-like fights) rather than the PvP where Jev's 24 ms shines, or the comparison with Hao AI Lab will look bad.

VIEWER-PLAYABLE ON muse.ai: muse.ai is Meta's (verified). A viewer could add a custom connector to a public remote MCP server we host (a 'Minecraft body' on our public Paper server) and tell their Muse to play. A laptop-hosted server is unreachable, so it must be cloud-hosted. Only US (maybe Canada) adults can use Muse, so most Douyin viewers cannot. In this path only the FlashEvolve-evolved skill is 'our project'; none of our serving systems run.

REUSE: MCJev (Apache-2.0) gives a ready mineflayer body and a POST /api/evaluate contract, so a Muse backend can be dropped in; this assumes Spark exposes logprobs (UNVERIFIED). rmalde/minecraft-agent already uses OpenRouter (Glimmer is listed there) but has no license, so avoid copying its code.

CLAIMS: we can claim 'Muse plays Minecraft with our FlashEvolve' once it has run. Do not claim 'first' until someone searches for prior Muse+Minecraft posts; I could not, because the web-search budget ran out.
